3bcfcccbe5.d: On 17 June in Kotah-ki-Serai near the Phool Bagh of Gwalior, a squadron of the 8th (King's Royal Irish) Hussars, under Captain Heneage, fought the large Indian force commanded by Rani Lakshmibai, who was trying to leave the area. The 8th Hussars charged into the Indian force, slaughtering 5,000 Indian soldiers, including any Indian "over the age of 16". They took two guns and continued the charge right through the Phool Bagh encampment. In this engagement, according to an eyewitness account, Rani Lakshmibai put on a sowar's uniform and attacked one of the hussars; she was unhorsed and also wounded, probably by his sabre. Shortly afterwards, as she sat bleeding by the roadside, she recognised the soldier and fired at him with a pistol, whereupon he "dispatched the young lady with his carbine".

3c259bd41c.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′44.11″.
3c259bd41c.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′44.11″, 0°57′39.80″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′13.45″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′18.80″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°56′57.57″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.15″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3d3b8b05de.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′41.63″.
3d3b8b05de.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′41.63″, 0°29′21.74″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′57.23″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′24.04″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′38.86″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′53.61″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3d4886a861.b: Observed on Śukla-Daśamī tithi of Vaiśākhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
3d4886a861.d:
The celestial wedding of Bhagavan Srinivasa and Devi Padmavati is a grand festival held annually in the month of Vaishakha. The beautifully adorned Parinayotsavam Mandapam, set amidst the Narayanagiri gardens, serves as the enchanting venue for this three-day event, celebrated under the moonlit sky. The festivities unfold on the auspicious days of Navami, Dashami, and Ekadashi in the month of Vaishakha, featuring Sri Malayappaswami, Shri Venkateshwara's festival deity. Each day, he makes a grand entrance on different Vahanas: the Gaja (elephant), Ashva (horse), and Garuda (eagle), while Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi grace the event on separate palanquins.

Following the wedding rituals at the Parinayotsava Mandapam, a traditional 'Koluvu' gathering takes place, filled with the recitation of Vedic hymns and devotional songs. Bhagavan, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, then majestically returns to the temple.

Each day's festivities are marked by unique traditional rituals. On the first day, the arrival of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami on the celestial Gaja Vahanam, along with his consorts on their palanquins, is a sight to behold. The traditional wedding ceremony is conducted, where Bhagavan is seated in the ornately decorated Parinaya Mandapam, with his consorts positioned opposite him.

The ceremony includes several traditional rituals such as Edurukolu (mutual reception), Pula Bantata (game of flower balls), and Vastra Dharanam (offering of new clothes). These customs are observed over all three days. The grand finale of the divine marriage is marked by a spectacular display of fireworks, adding to the ceremony's splendor. The event concludes with a procession where Bhagavan Malayappa Swami, along with Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi, return to the main temple.

3d9e9aedbb.b: Observed on Ārdrā nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
3d9e9aedbb.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

In the region of Tirunavalur in Tirumuraipadi, there lived a devout Adi Shaiva named Sadayanar, whose lineage was known for its deep devotion to Bhagavan Shiva. Sadayanar, embodying the same piety and dedication, was married to Isaijnaniyar, a woman equally devoted to Bhagavan. Their virtuous past actions blessed them with a divine child, who was none other than Sundaramurthi Nayanmar.

The child's striking beauty caught the attention of Narasinga Munaiyar, the local king, who expressed a desire to raise the child himself. Demonstrating their detachment from worldly attachments, Sadayanar and Isaijnaniyar willingly entrusted their child to the king without hesitation. This couple exemplified the ideal life of householders, focusing on spiritual devotion and ultimately earning the grace of the Divine.
3d9e9aedbb.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌥𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌧𑌾𑌦𑌗𑌲𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌆𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍀𑌠𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌃॥௬௬॥

3dfb040cbf.b: Observed on Śukla-Ēkādaśī tithi of Pauṣaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti). The event occurred in 4625 (Kali era).
3dfb040cbf.d: Heaps of merits embodied as the son of Purāri and Śrīmati of the town Aśmaśālapura on the banks of the sweet river Maṇimukta, Aruṇagiri governed the preceptorship of the Pīṭha surrounded by the four oceans as preceptor candracūḍa. Thus having imparted the teachings to me, the insignificant among disciples and guiding me through all aspects relating to the Pīṭha, the preceptor who stayed at the Maṭha for only six years at siddhi in a moment, He merged in the Eternal Bliss, the Supreme Effulgence, devoid of calamities at the dawn of eleventh day of bright fortnight of the Mārgaśīrṣa month in the year Āṅgīrasa at Kañci.

3e34e47151.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′14.81″.
3e34e47151.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°36′14.81″, 0°36′01.39″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°15′32.28″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.71, elongation 25°42′15.21″ W). śukraḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°39′17.48″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.87, elongation 25°39′40.81″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
3e34e47151.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

3e7dad150d.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′01.76″.
3e7dad150d.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′01.76″, 0°40′56.90″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°06′36.52″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.17, elongation 16°01′12.06″ E). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°47′38.28″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.85, elongation 16°04′48.93″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3e89372262.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈3.8 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
3e89372262.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.32 (parimāṇa ≈3.8 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:38►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
3e89372262.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

3ed4c8f3b9.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′53.93″.
3ed4c8f3b9.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′53.93″, 0°33′43.61″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′21.41″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′15.51″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′15.34″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′37.92″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3f1e40c294.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈5.0 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
3f1e40c294.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.42 (parimāṇa ≈5.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:24►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
3f1e40c294.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3f6cae80a7.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′21.00″.
3f6cae80a7.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′21.00″, 0°37′03.45″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′42.75″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′45.44″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′03.75″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°38′02.57″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

3fbaef4ed7.d:
Sikh Guru Govind Singh's  9 & 6 year old kids, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were killed by Mogols in Sirhind Fort. First they tried to bury them alive, then killed. They'd refusing to convert to Islam.

This verse is sung about them:

“Turk bhay mare naahin  
Hindu raha marhahi  
kaal sabhahun ko khai hai taantey ab tum vichaar karo chaar din Jeevan kay het hum dharma kyon gavaai hai.” 

> “We will not die just for the fear of Turks, we will remain Hindus till death, Time will kill all, why should we lose our Dharma for this life of four days.” 

- Panth Prakash, Giani Gian Singh.

**Timing**  
1705-01-07 gregorian = 1704-12-27 julian = pUrNimAnta pauSha 13 is mentioned. Their grandmother, Gurjar Kaur, also died on the same day or next, it seems.

A fair is held 11-13 Poh in commemoration. Indian government, under Narendra Modi, declared as vIra-bAla-divasa Dec 25 Gregorian in their memory - based on being bricked on Dec 25 Julian.

3fffe88dd7.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

The 43rd Nayanmar was a Vaishya, and resided in Pennagadam, a part of the Chola kingdom. He was known for his devout service in the local temple and held a deep reverence for Shiva Bhaktas, seeing the divine presence of Bhagavan Shiva in them. His wife also actively supported him in these spiritual endeavours.

On one occasion, though, a man who had previously been a servant of the Nayanmar visited his house, disguised as a Shiva Bhakta. True to his devotional nature, the Nayanmar warmly welcomed the visitor, offering the traditional respect of washing his feet and venerating him. However, his wife, recognizing the man as their former servant, did not participate in the worship with the same enthusiasm.

Perceiving his wife's reluctance as a lack of devotion, the Nayanmar, in a drastic and shocking act, severed her hand. He then proceeded to continue his worship of the disguised Bhakta with undeterred focus. Through this extreme form of spiritual practice and dedication, he ultimately achieved union with the divine.
3fffe88dd7.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society
